# Tampa Theatre Guide: 5 Things to Know Before You Go to the 1926 Movie Palace

Tampa Theatre is the 1926 movie palace at 711 N. Franklin Street, downtown, between Zack and Polk. People search for it a few ways: tampa theatre florida, tampa theatre tampa fl, tampa florida theatre. It is the same building. I spell it "theatre" with the British ending on purpose, because the American "theater" spelling pulls in multiplexes and other rooms downtown that have nothing to do with this place. If a guide sends you to a different address, it is the wrong building. Here is what I would tell a friend before they drove over.

![Tampa Theatre exterior on North Franklin Street in downtown Tampa, with the marquee lit at dusk](https://images.pexels.com/photos/31234108/pexels-photo-31234108.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Mike Norris](https://www.pexels.com/@mike-norris-2149008874) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/fountain-square-theatre-at-night-in-indianapolis-31234108/)*

## Short on Time?

🎬 Tampa Theatre is at 711 N. Franklin Street. The box office number is (813) 274-8286.

- Buy tickets only through the theatre's own eTix system or at the window. They do not take ticket orders by phone.
- Do not assume the lot next to the building is theirs. Two private lots nearby are run by a separate company, and the theatre does not own them.
- The big auditorium with the painted night sky was scheduled to close from March 10 through the end of September 2026 for restoration, timed to the building's 100th anniversary this month. Call before you promise anyone that hall.
- The balcony and mezzanine are reached by stairs only. If someone cannot climb, pick the orchestra level.
- No backpacks, no outside food or drink, and no smoking or vaping inside.

## 1. The painted night sky over Tampa Theatre

Everyone comes for the ceiling, and it is the first thing that gets you when you walk in. The room is built to feel like you are sitting outdoors under a night sky. There are stars overhead, gargoyles along the walls, and statues in the stage alcoves. The styles are mixed on purpose: Mediterranean, Baroque, and a lot of other centuries piled together, the way a rich person's garden might have been put together in the 1920s.

The building opened on October 15, 1926. John Eberson designed it, and Paramount built it. The idea came from Florida winters. Eberson had seen Italian gardens and Spanish patios, and he wanted a movie house that felt like one of those places at night, with the sky above you instead of a flat proscenium box. That is what they call an atmospheric theatre, and this one is still standing with most of its look intact, which is the reason people drive across the bay for it.

The room was also a bit of a stunt in its day. It was the first commercial building in Tampa with air conditioning, which mattered a lot in a city where the August afternoons could flatten you. Talkies had not arrived yet, so the sound came from a big organ and an orchestra. A quarter got you in. I always think about that when I am sitting in a theater seat that has a cupholder built into the armrest, which I'll get to.

The building nearly did not make it. By the 1950s, suburbs and television had emptied out a lot of downtown palaces across the country, and this one fell on hard times too. In 1973 it was slated for demolition. The city council bought it instead, and it reopened to the public in January 1977. People point to that rescue as a model for saving an old theatre, and I think it still holds up. Today the building is run by a nonprofit, Tampa Theatre, Inc. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, and it became a Tampa City Landmark in 1988.

The historic auditorium has about 1,200 seats, and the theatre's own count puts it at 1,238. The place hosts close to a thousand events a year, so it is not a museum that happens to show films. You can see first-run movies, classics, concerts, tours, and special events in the same room.

Now the closure, because it matters for timing. The theatre's plan calls for paint, plaster, infrastructure, and the original fixtures in the main hall to be worked on, and the Historic Duncan Auditorium was scheduled to be closed from March 10 through the end of September 2026. The work was meant to be finished for the 100th anniversary in October. The good news is that the theatre was already selling October shows when I last looked, so the hall should be back. I would still call the box office before you buy, though. Dates can slide on a project like this, and it is a bad surprise to show up expecting a star ceiling and find a smaller room.

If the big hall is not available, the John T. Taylor Screening Room is the other option. It is a 43-seat microcinema in the storefront next to the Franklin Street box office. It debuted in June 2024, and it is how the theatre kept showing movies during the construction. It is small, but it is a legitimate way to see a film in the building, and it is close to the main entrance.

![Painted star ceiling, gargoyles, and stage alcove statues inside the Historic Duncan Auditorium at Tampa Theatre](https://images.pexels.com/photos/33939862/pexels-photo-33939862.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Michael D Beckwith](https://www.pexels.com/@michael-d-beckwith-2150568551) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/historic-dome-ceiling-at-the-old-bailey-london-33939862/)*

## 2. The Wurlitzer and the organ

The Mighty Wurlitzer is the other reason people stop in. It has about 1,400 pipes, and it is the sound the building was built around in the years before talkies. When sound films took over, the organ was moved out and eventually ended up at a church. It might have stayed gone for good, but volunteers from the Central Florida Theatre Organ Society brought it back to the theatre in the 1980s. It is still operating.

Artist in residence Steven Ball and those volunteers play it. The theatre says the organ is played before film screenings and at special silent-film events. I would not promise you organ music at every show, though. If you are going specifically to hear it, look at the event listing for the night you plan to go, or ask the box office. A silent film with live organ is one of the best things you can do in this room, and it is worth planning around if you can.

What I like about hearing it is how physical it is. The sound fills the auditorium from the front, and you feel it in the seat, not just in your ears. Even if you are not an organ person, it is hard to sit there and not be a little impressed.

![Wurlitzer theatre organ console on stage at Tampa Theatre in downtown Tampa](https://images.pexels.com/photos/39591668/pexels-photo-39591668.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Dmitry Romanoff](https://www.pexels.com/@dmitry-romanoff-1151933996) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/elegant-interior-of-a-historic-italian-opera-house-39591668/)*

## 3. Tickets, eTix, and the lookalike sellers

This is the section I wish more visitors read first, because the trouble I have seen usually starts with tickets.

Tampa Theatre does not take ticket orders over the phone. You buy through eTix, which is the theatre's official seller, or at the window. When you buy online, the confirmation email comes from confirmation@etix.com. If it is not in your inbox, check spam. The theatre suggests adding the eTix and theatre addresses to your safe senders list so the next message does not get lost.

If you are picking up tickets at will call, you need a photo ID. If someone else is picking up for you, they need a copy of the buyer's ID. Mailed tickets only go out 30 days ahead of the show, and only within 100 miles of the theatre. Tickets are not refundable, and the theatre's own advice is to order only when you are sure you can make it.

If a show is cancelled, the theatre emails about a refund, a credit, or an exchange. If a show is only postponed, the promoter decides whether money comes back. Keep that in mind for concerts and live events, which are run by outside promoters.

Now the part that hurts people. Third-party resellers copy the theatre's look, use similar branding, and inflate the price. The theatre defines a broker as someone buying to resell for more than $1 over face value, and it points to Florida statute 817.36 on this. The practical problem is simple. A reseller's ticket may look real and still not get you through the door. I have seen people argue at the front with staff who cannot help them, and that is a bad way to start a date night. Only a real Tampa Theatre ticket works at the door, so buy from the theatre or its official eTix page.

Some other ticket details: children under 3 are free for general-seating events. For reserved-seating shows, everyone needs a ticket, including infants. The theatre leaves it to parents to decide whether a particular show is a good idea for a kid, and it says so openly. If a tour has an age limit, the limit is stated with that event.

The box office on Franklin Street opens at 10:00 a.m. on weekdays and stays staffed until 30 minutes after the last show starts. On evenings and weekends, it opens at least 30 minutes before the first show and closes 30 minutes after the last one starts. Holidays and live events change the schedule, so check before you go. For live shows, will call is usually a table set up outside. If you have questions, you can reach the box office at (813) 274-8286 or email gargoyles@tampatheatre.org.

![Tampa Theatre box office window on North Franklin Street, with the marquee overhead](https://images.pexels.com/photos/6304763/pexels-photo-6304763.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Bekir Donmez](https://www.pexels.com/@bekirdonmeez) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/a-woman-walking-in-front-of-the-ed-mirvish-theatre-6304763/)*

## 4. Parking, transit, and getting there

There is no Tampa Theatre garage, so plan your park before you leave home. Street meters near the theatre are enforced from 8:00 a.m. to midnight, seven days a week. You can pay at the sidewalk station or through one of the four city apps. If you have a valid disabled parking plate or permit, you can park at the meters for up to four hours free, and you do not have to start a session.

The closest public lot the theatre names is the Royal Regional Lot at 1200 N. Tampa Street. Enter from N. Tampa Street. It is about 0.3 mile away, roughly a 7-minute walk. It is a surface lot, not a garage. The rate can go up on nights with downtown events, so check before you park. The closest garage is the William F. Poe Garage, about three blocks west at 800 N. Ashley Drive, between Curtis Hixon and the John F. Germany Public Library. Same warning applies: event pricing can change. The theatre suggests using ParkMobile for payment.

Now the lot that fools people. Two private lots are run by 717 Parking Enterprises. One sits next to the theatre, and the other is southwest of the building, between Zack and Twiggs. Tampa Theatre does not own either of them. The theatre's advice is to read the signs, pay the machine, or you can be ticketed or towed. You can pay those lots through the ParkMobile app or the 717 app, which saves you the kiosk line. I have watched people walk straight into the adjacent lot because it looks like theatre parking. It is not.

If you are not driving, the downtown DASH bus costs $2 a person, and the nearest DASH on-demand hub is less than a block away at Franklin and Polk. Lime and Spin scooters are an option too. HART buses run through downtown, and the TECO Line Streetcar is free, with the theatre listing its service as running from 7:00 a.m. until late.

Driving in, the simplest route is to get to Ashley and then turn left on Zack. From I-275 south, take exit 45A. From I-275 north coming from St. Petersburg, take exit 44. From the Crosstown, take the Kennedy Boulevard exit, exit 8, then turn right on Ashley and left on Zack.

One more thing about parking. People who come downtown for the aquarium often park and assume the theatre is next door. It is not a stroll from 701 Channelside in the heat. It is a streetcar ride or a long walk, and in Tampa summer, a long walk is no joke. Plan the route before you commit to the parking spot.

![Street parking meters on North Franklin Street in downtown Tampa near the theatre](https://images.pexels.com/photos/9844320/pexels-photo-9844320.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Raphael Loquellano](https://www.pexels.com/@loquellano) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/parking-meter-on-a-parking-9844320/)*

## 5. Seats, access, and the stairs

The house was reseated, which the theatre says was the first time in 40 years. All of the more than 1,200 seats now have cupholders. The orchestra level got about six extra inches of legroom, which is a real difference if you are tall. The mezzanine and balcony kept the 1926 spacing, and that spacing is tight. If you have long legs, this is the part of the building where you will notice it.

The mezzanine has bistro tables set between every other seat, so you can put a drink down without balancing it on a knee. The balcony has two banquettes meant to seat four across. On general-admission shows, they are first-come. On reserved-seating shows, you have to buy them as a block of four.

Accessibility is important here, so read this part carefully. There is no elevator. The orchestra level and the lobby are accessible. The accessible restrooms are at the rear of the orchestra. The mezzanine and balcony are reached by stairs only. Wheelchair and companion seats are first-come on general-admission films. For reserved-seating shows, call the box office to choose seats. Some aisle seats have swing-away armrests. The theatre offers assistive listening for all films. Captioning and audio description are available only when the film has been encoded for them. The devices are picked up at concessions.

My honest advice is this. The balcony is the hot, crowded, stair-only part of the house, and on a busy night it can feel like the warm air has nowhere to go. If someone in your group cannot manage stairs, buy orchestra seats and skip the upper levels entirely. The room is still beautiful from the floor, and you will not feel like you are missing the show.

![Orchestra seating with cupholders and the stage visible inside Tampa Theatre in downtown Tampa](https://images.pexels.com/photos/6639844/pexels-photo-6639844.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Gu Bra](https://www.pexels.com/@gu-bra-11680150) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/empty-hall-in-theatre-6639844/)*

## Useful Things to Know

Bags are the first thing that trips people up. No backpacks are allowed. Purses and small bags are checked, and the building uses metal detectors. Outside food and drink are not permitted. Professional cameras, laser pointers, and noisemakers are not allowed. Weapons are not permitted under state law. Smoking and vaping are not allowed inside, and that includes an e-cigarette in the building. If you are asked to leave for that reason, there is no refund. The theatre can mark your ticket for re-entry if you step outside, but do not count on it. Plan to finish your vape before you walk in.

Concessions cover the basics: popcorn, candy, and a full bar with beer, wine, and cocktails. There is also salami and cheese, and coffee. 🍿 If you want a real dinner before a show, plan to walk. The lobby is not a restaurant. The theatre points people to nearby places like Bavaro's, Ulele, and Oxford Exchange. It also lists partner hotel rates at a few downtown and Channel District hotels, though those depend on availability, so ask when you book.

On the event side, the theatre is selling a book, Tampa Theatre: A Century of Stories, by Andrew Huse, from University Press of Florida. It has 272 pages, the publication date is September 22, 2026, and the retail price is $30. There is also an event at the theatre on October 15 with admission at $26. That $26 is for the event, not for a regular movie ticket, so do not show up at the window expecting a $26 film.

Finally, the matinee is still the best way to use this building. The place was air-conditioned in 1926 so people could get out of the Florida heat, and that is still the point. A weekday afternoon show in the orchestra, with the sky overhead and the cold air coming through, is about as good as it gets in this town. 🎹 If you catch a silent film with the organ going, you will understand why people keep coming back.

## FAQ

### Is Tampa Theatre the same place as Tampa Theater?

Tampa Theatre, the 1926 movie palace, is at 711 N. Franklin Street in downtown Tampa. People often spell it "theater" when they search, but many results with that spelling point to multiplexes and other rooms downtown. If the address is not 711 Franklin Street, it is probably not this place.

### Can I buy Tampa Theatre tickets over the phone?

No. The theatre does not take ticket orders by phone. You can buy through eTix, the official seller, or at the box office window on Franklin Street. Check your spam folder for the confirmation email, which comes from confirmation@etix.com.

### Is the Wurlitzer organ played at every screening?

No. The organ is played before film screenings and at special silent-film events, but not at every show. If you want to hear it, check the listing for the date you plan to attend, or call the box office at (813) 274-8286.

### Is the big auditorium with the painted sky open?

The historic Duncan Auditorium was scheduled to close from March 10 through the end of September 2026 for restoration, timed to the building's 100th anniversary in October. The theatre was already selling October shows, so it should be open, but call the box office before you go and confirm which room your show is in. The John T. Taylor Screening Room, a 43-seat space next to the box office, is the smaller option.

### Where should I park for Tampa Theatre?

There is no theatre garage. Street meters are enforced from 8:00 a.m. to midnight, seven days a week. The Royal Regional Lot at 1200 N. Tampa Street is about a 7-minute walk, and the William F. Poe Garage at 800 N. Ashley Drive is about three blocks west. Avoid the two private lots run by 717 Parking Enterprises, which the theatre does not own.

### Are there elevators to the balcony and mezzanine?

No. There is no elevator. The orchestra level and the lobby are accessible, with accessible restrooms at the rear of the orchestra. The mezzanine and balcony are reached by stairs only. If someone in your group cannot climb stairs, buy orchestra seats.

### Do children need their own tickets?

It depends on the type of seating. Children under 3 are free for general-seating events. For reserved-seating shows, everyone needs a ticket, including infants. The theatre leaves it to parents to decide whether a particular show is right for a child, and any age limit on a tour is stated with that event.

## Final Thoughts

Tampa Theatre is one of the best places in this city to see a movie, and it is also a building worth seeing on its own terms. The painted sky, the organ, and the air conditioning that once made it a novelty are still there. The things that cause trouble are almost all practical: which ticket to buy, which lot to park in, which stairs to avoid, and whether the big hall is open that night. Get those right, and the rest of the visit is easy. Call the box office if you have any doubt, buy your tickets from the official seller, and give yourself time to walk in from wherever you park.

body:
# Tampa Zoo Guide: ZooTampa at Lowry Park Realm by Realm

If you say "tampa zoo" around here, you will get a few different answers. Some people mean ZooTampa at Lowry Park, the animal park on the west side of town. Some mean the coaster park down the road that also keeps animals. A few say "zoo tampa," "zoo at Tampa," or "Tampa Florida zoo" and mean the same place. I have been going to the Lowry Park zoo for years, and this is my walk through it: what to see, what to skip, how the tickets and parking work, and what I wish someone had told me the first time.

![ZooTampa entrance at Lowry Park with the palm-lined walkway on a bright morning](https://images.pexels.com/photos/31039041/pexels-photo-31039041.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [DΛVΞ GΛRCIΛ](https://www.pexels.com/@davegarcia) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/lush-palm-lined-pathway-at-prestigious-campus-31039041/)*

## Short on Time?

ZooTampa is at 1101 W. Sligh Avenue in Tampa. It is a real zoo with a lot of ground to cover, a natural area around the edges, and a manatee rehab center on site. Go early. The heat is the thing that will wear you down, not the walking. Book any signature encounter ahead of time, because it is reservation-only. Park with the understanding that non-members pay a daily parking fee. Check the hours the morning you go, because special event nights run on different clocks.

Do not confuse it with Busch Gardens. The coaster park is a separate ticket, a separate day, and a separate trip. If you want the animals, you want the zoo. If you want the drops, you want the other place. If you want both, plan two days. CityPASS sells them as separate choices, along with The Florida Aquarium, MOSI, and Glazer Children's Museum, if you are building a bigger itinerary.

The rest of this piece walks through the six areas of the zoo in the order I usually see them, then covers the practical stuff people get wrong.

## 1. Manatee Circle: the front door of the Tampa zoo

Manatee Circle is the first stretch you hit after the gate, and I like starting there because it sets the tone for the whole park. The Canopy Aviary is right inside, and the birds are loud in the good way. The Macaw Flyover runs around the circle, so you will look up more than you expect. Manatee Fountains are a nice place to stop, and Macaw's Landing is one of the indoor breaks that makes a difference on a hot day. It is also a good place to get a drink of ice water while you figure out where you want to go first.

The real reason to come early is the Manatee Critical Care Center, the David A. Straz, Jr. Manatee Critical Care Center, which sits on site. By the zoo's own count, it is one of only two contracted, federally permitted manatee rehab centers in the country, and it has treated more than 600 manatees since 1991, most of them released. Seeing the work up close makes the rest of the park feel less like a stroll and more like a working place. Florida Waters, the area with underwater manatee viewing, is nearby, and it is worth the time if you have kids who get bored by standing still.

I would give this area a solid 45 minutes on a first visit, longer if you like birds.

![Manatee Critical Care Center at ZooTampa with a manatee resting in a rehab pool](https://images.pexels.com/photos/13277592/pexels-photo-13277592.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Jakub Pabis](https://www.pexels.com/@jakub-pabis-147246622) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/african-manatee-eating-while-swimming-underwater-13277592/)*

## 2. Asia: tigers, bears, and rhinos, with a feeding extra 🐅

Asia is where the zoo starts to feel like a zoo in the old sense. The Malayan tiger, the sun bear, and the greater one-horned rhino are the big names here. The enclosures are built so you can see the animals without a lot of barriers getting in the way, and on a cool morning they are often more active than they are at midday.

Lorikeet Landing is the part that catches people. Feeding the lorikeets is a small extra fee, and it is a fun thing to do with kids, but it is not free and it is not something you should assume is included. There is also a Sulawesi aviary here, which is quieter than the lorikeet area and gives you a chance to slow down for a few minutes.

If you are someone who likes to read signs, take a minute to read the ones at the tiger and bear areas. The animals are the point, and the signs are how you learn what you are looking at.

![Malayan tiger resting in a shaded Asia exhibit at ZooTampa](https://images.pexels.com/photos/32522599/pexels-photo-32522599.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Ayberk Mirza](https://www.pexels.com/@holoshuriken) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/majestic-tiger-swimming-in-natural-habitat-32522599/)*

## 3. Florida: panthers, bears, manatees, and the wild animals you should not approach 🐊

Florida is my favorite area and the one I think people underestimate most. The panthers, black bears, red wolves, and alligators are all here, and the manatees are the reason many people come. The reptile hall is a good break from the sun, and Otter Oasis is one of the places where you can watch animals that tend to be on the move.

I want to be clear about one thing. The zoo describes the grounds as a 67-acre natural park, and alligators, snakes, and other native wildlife live on the property outside the zoo's care. Do not approach the ponds or the tall grass. This is the part I noticed people getting wrong most often. They see an animal in the grass and assume it is an exhibit animal, and it is not. The wild ones are wild. Stay on the paths, keep kids close, and do not try to get a better photo by stepping off the boardwalk.

Stingray Shores, the touch pool, is also in or near this part of the park. The rules there are about being gentle and following staff direction, and I would take those rules seriously.

![Alligator resting by a pond edge along a shaded Florida boardwalk at ZooTampa](https://images.pexels.com/photos/36508412/pexels-photo-36508412.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Matthew Hernandez](https://www.pexels.com/@mhaltiery) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/american-alligator-on-wooden-surface-36508412/)*

## 4. Australia: the cool-off realm with splash pad, coasters, and the koala clubhouse

Australia is where you go when it is hot, and it is hot most of the year. Billabong Splash Pad is the big cool-off spot. It is presented by Bank of America, and when I last looked at the hours, it ran from 9:30 to 5:00 with a 99-person cap. You need non-slip shoes, and you cannot bring food or glass into the splash pad. It also closes at dusk on event nights, so do not plan on it for a late evening visit without checking.

The rides here are Aussie Trek, Boomer's Flyin' Bananas, and the Tasmanian Tiger Coaster. All three have height rules, and all three can be shut down when the weather or the track conditions turn. If a ride has a line and a closed sign, that is not a sign you did something wrong. It is the zoo keeping people safe.

Koala Clubhouse is the playground, and it is a good stop for kids who are tired of looking at animals through glass. Lil' Joey's, presented by TGH Muma Children's Hospital, is the indoor family stop, and it is the one I would point to if you have a toddler and a summer afternoon that is getting away from you.

The Outpost and Boomerang Bar both have complimentary ice water. I mention that because the cost of a drink adds up fast, and it is good to know which places give you water for free.

![Billabong Splash Pad in Australia at ZooTampa with children playing under the water sprays](https://images.pexels.com/photos/10601708/pexels-photo-10601708.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Ouça e  Relaxe](https://www.pexels.com/@rogeriopritzke) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/water-park-for-children-in-a-festival-10601708/)*

## 5. Africa: the long walk, the safari ride, and the signature encounters 🦒

Africa is the longest walk in the zoo, and it has the most animals I think people hope to see up close. Elephants, giraffes, shoebills, white rhinos, painted dogs, okapi, and pygmy hippos all live in this part of the park. Plan for distance. If you are pushing a stroller or carrying a tired kid, allow more time than you think you need.

Expedition Wild Africa is the Land Rover ride. Kids under 56 inches have to ride with an adult. The zoo says rides, including that safari and Roaring Springs, are not an extra charge, and that is the good news. The signature encounters are a different story.

The signature encounters are giraffe, white rhino, giant tortoise, penguin, koala, stingray in-water, and manatee behind-the-scenes. They are reservation-only and limited, and kids under 18 need to be with a paying adult. Buy them ahead. If you show up without a reservation and hope to squeeze one in, you will likely be disappointed. Touching is not guaranteed. The animal decides whether it wants to come close, and the staff will not push it. I think that is the right approach, even if it is frustrating when your kid is standing there with a sign that says "touch me."

Savanna Oasis is an indoor break in Africa and it has complimentary ice water. If you are in the middle of the long walk in July, that stop can save the afternoon.

![Giraffes at the feeding platform in the Africa area of ZooTampa](https://images.pexels.com/photos/28615943/pexels-photo-28615943.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Sergio Zhukov](https://www.pexels.com/@triemli) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/two-giraffes-feeding-in-zoo-enclosure-28615943/)*

## 6. Primates and the carousel: the part people forget

Primates is its own realm, and I think a lot of people walk past it without stopping. Take a few minutes. The primate area is one of the quieter corners of the park, and the animals are often more interesting to watch than the ones in the big-name exhibits.

The carousel is included with admission, and the animals on it are not for adults. Adults cannot ride the animals, so if you are an adult with a child who wants to ride, you will be watching from the side. The carousel is near the penguins, which is also one of the spots the zoo lists as a mister area, so it is a good place to cool down if you need it.

The Saunders Theater and ZooVentures Theater are where the wildlife chats happen. These are not separate show tickets. You can sit in on them as part of your visit, and they are a good way to rest your feet while learning something new. I would plan a chat into your afternoon if you have young kids who are getting restless.

![Primate enclosure at ZooTampa with a monkey climbing a rope structure](https://images.pexels.com/photos/33977909/pexels-photo-33977909.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&dpr=2&h=650&w=940)
*Photo by [Regan Dsouza](https://www.pexels.com/@regan-dsouza-1315522347) on [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/close-up-of-a-squirrel-monkey-in-a-zoo-enclosure-33977909/)*

## Useful Things to Know

**Tickets.** Reservations are not required for a normal visit. They are required for signature encounters, and I would book those before you leave the house. You do not need a printed ticket. A phone barcode works, and so do Apple Pay, Google Pay, Samsung Pay, or the zoo's app. If the email never shows up, check your spam folder for anything with "ZooTampa" in it. You can also bring the order number, or your name and a photo ID, to the ticket window. That window is where I saw people struggling most, because it sits in the same entrance crush as bag check.

**Prices.** This is the messy part, and I want to be honest about it. The zoo's own numbers do not agree with each other. At full price, general admission is listed at $51.95 for ages 12 and up and $41.95 for ages 3 to 11. Elsewhere, the same full prices show up next to $48.95 and $38.95, and the zoo says buying your single-day ticket ahead saves $3. The CityPASS comparison price I saw was $53.95 for adults and $43.95 for children. The joint ticket with The Florida Aquarium, called ZooQuarium, shows the zoo at $51.95 and $41.95 inside a bundle with a sale price, but parking is extra, it is not good for special events, and its voucher rules say two different things about how long it is valid. I would not trust anyone who quotes you just one of these numbers. Check the price the morning you go, on the zoo's own ticketing page, and do not rely on a number you saw months ago.

**Discounts.** There is no free birthday admission. Active-duty military and veterans get $4 off per ticket, up to four tickets, with ID, and that discount is only available at the front-gate windows. Seniors get $2 off at the window. The zoo says it does not discount Florida residents, AARP, EBT, AAA, teachers, or students. Groups of 15 or more are quoted, not sold at the walk-up price. The AZA reciprocal benefit applies to single-day tickets only, not memberships or Zoo Fun, and the rules are set by the other zoo's family definition rather than ZooTampa's.

**Zoo Fun versus a membership.** This is the other knot. A Zoo Fun ticket is free repeat admission, with blockouts. The zoo has given two different end dates for it. Some of the information I saw says it runs through the end of 2026, and some says through the end of 2027. The blockouts I saw for 2026 include October 10, 17, and 24 after 4:00 p.m. during Creatures of the Night, and November 27 and 28, 2026, including Christmas in the Wild. Blockouts I saw for 2027 include March 20 through 28. Blockouts apply to repeat visits, not your first use. If you have already used your Zoo Fun ticket, a blockout day means a small extra fee or an upgrade, and you should go to the window and ask what the current deal is. A membership is a different product. It comes with free parking, guest privileges, discounts at dining and the shop, member events, and reciprocal admission. The membership prices and end years also do not match everywhere I looked. I would not memorize either version. Ask at the window or on the phone at (813) 935-8552 before you decide.

**Parking.** Non-members pay a daily parking fee of $10 through ParkMobile, and that includes Zoo Fun holders. Members park free, but the license plate has to be registered, or you can end up with a citation. Paid parking for non-members started January 5, 2026, so do not assume the lot is still free from an older visit.

**Hours.** The standing hours are 9:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., seven days a week. The zoo is closed on Thanksgiving. On Christmas Eve it runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. and it is closed on Christmas Day. Special event days are different. I saw a Creatures of the Night notice that listed 9:30 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. while the standing hours were 5:00 p.m. Creatures of the Night is the long one, so check the hours the day you go, not from memory. There was also a September notice about an early closure for an AZA conference. That date has passed, but it is exactly the kind of leftover notice that causes people to show up to a closed gate, so check the most recent information before you drive over.

**Front gate construction.** The front gate area is under construction. There is a temporary entrance and exit while the arrival plaza is rebuilt. Do not follow an old map pin to the front doors. Look at the signs when you arrive, and give yourself a few extra minutes to find the right entrance.

**Re-entry and food.** If you leave the park, you get a wristband from the exit attendant to come back in. Outside food is tight. The picnic area is outside the park, next to the main parking lot. There is no alcohol allowed there. You cannot bring plastic bags, straws, or coffee lids. Soft coolers over a small size are not allowed either. The zoo says the restrictions are for the animals, and I think that is probably true.

**Bag check.** Every bag is inspected at the entrance. Leave the extra stuff in the car. The more you carry, the longer the line, and the more likely you are to be standing in the sun while you wait.

**Heat.** Heat is the real limiter at this zoo, not the walking. The zoo's advice is to come early, when the animals are out and the air is better. Bring sunscreen and a hat, drink water, and use the misters. The named mister spots include Australia by the Koala Clubhouse and Aussie Trek, Africa by the hogs, giraffes, and white rhinos, the carousel near the penguins, and Florida by the gators, red wolves, Roaring Springs, and the flamingos. The cooling attractions are Roaring Springs, Billabong, and Manatee Fountains. The indoor breaks are Macaw's Landing and Savanna Oasis. The ZooTampa app has an Escape the Heat section that is worth looking at before you go. If someone in your group is in trouble, any staff member can call on-site medical. Do not wait to ask for help. 💧

**Weather.** The Not-So-Perfect Weather Program is not a blanket rain check. It applies only to tickets bought through a preferred reseller. It covers heavy rain and lightning lasting more than an hour, a heat index of 110 or higher, or temperatures under 50. You have to ask at Guest Services the same day, with your original ticket in hand, and the return ticket is one admission good for 30 days. Otherwise the zoo is open rain or shine. Rides close when the weather turns. The splash pad closes too. Plan for a plan B on a stormy afternoon, and keep an eye on the forecast the morning you go.

**What people get wrong.** The most common mistake I see is arriving at noon with no water, hitting the bag line in the heat, and then realizing the encounter they wanted was reservation-only and the coaster is wet. Avoid all three by coming early, bringing water in a small bag, and booking your encounters before you leave the house.

## FAQ

### Is the tampa zoo the same as Busch Gardens?

No. ZooTampa at Lowry Park is a zoo. Busch Gardens Tampa Bay is a coaster park that also keeps animals. They are different tickets, in different parts of town, and you will need a separate day for each. The mix-up is common, and I understand why, but if you want the animals, you want ZooTampa, and if you want the big rides, you want Busch Gardens.

### Where is the zoo, and what is the address?

ZooTampa at Lowry Park is at 1101 W. Sligh Avenue, Tampa, FL 33604. The phone number is (813) 935-8552. Because of the front gate construction, look for the temporary entrance and exit signs when you arrive rather than relying on an old map pin.

### How long should I plan to spend there?

For a first visit, I would plan at least four to five hours if you want to see most of the zoo at a reasonable pace. Families with young kids often need longer, and anyone who is booking a signature encounter or sitting in on a wildlife chat should add time around those. If the heat is high, plan for shorter stretches in the shade and longer breaks in the indoor spots.

### Do I need a reservation to visit?

You do not need a reservation for a normal visit. You do need one for signature encounters like giraffe, white rhino, giant tortoise, penguin, koala, stingray in-water, and manatee behind-the-scenes. Those are limited, so book them before you go. Kids under 18 need to be with a paying adult.

### Is parking free?

Not for most people. Non-members pay a daily parking fee of $10 through ParkMobile, and that includes Zoo Fun holders. Members park free, but the license plate has to be registered. Paid parking for non-members started January 5, 2026.

### Can I bring food into the zoo?

You can bring some food, but outside food is limited. The picnic area is outside the park by the main parking lot, and it does not allow alcohol. Plastic bags, straws, coffee lids, and soft coolers over a small size are not allowed inside. Plan to eat at one of the on-site spots or to leave the park and come back with a wristband from the exit attendant.

### What should I do if it rains or the heat gets bad?

Use the cooling spots and indoor breaks. Roaring Springs, Billabong, and Manatee Fountains help with the heat. Macaw's Landing and Savanna Oasis are your indoor options, and both have complimentary ice water. If the weather turns severe, check whether your ticket qualifies under the Not-So-Perfect Weather Program. It is not a general rain check, so ask at Guest Services the same day with your original ticket.

### Are there any discounts I should know about?

There is no free birthday admission. Active-duty military and veterans get $4 off per ticket, up to four tickets, with ID, at the front-gate windows. Seniors get $2 off at the window. The zoo says it does not discount Florida residents, AARP, EBT, AAA, teachers, or students. Ticket prices have shown some differences across the zoo's own pages, so confirm the current price before you go.

## Final Thoughts

I like ZooTampa at Lowry Park more than I expected to the first time I walked in, and I still find something new on most visits. The manatee rehab center is the part I think about after I leave. The Florida area is my favorite for the wild animals that are not supposed to be a show. Africa is the long walk I stop complaining about once I get to the giraffes.

It is not a perfect place. The ticket prices do not line up cleanly, the membership and Zoo Fun dates do not agree everywhere, and the heat will test you. Come early, book your encounters, bring water, and check the hours and the parking before you leave the house. If you do those things, you will have a good day, and you will be glad you came to the zoo and not the coaster park down the road.
